title: Grep and Text Search Techniques
learning_objectives: Use grep to search for patterns in files and command output effectively
Apply basic and extended regular expressions with egrep for complex pattern matching
Chain grep with other commands using pipes for powerful text filtering workflows
Customize grep output with context lines, line numbers, and color highlighting
Distinguish between grep, egrep, and fgrep and know when to use each variant

post_assessment.question: Which grep flag displays 2 lines of context before and 3 lines after each match?
post_assessment.explanation: The -B flag (Before) specifies lines before the match, and -A (After) specifies lines after. -B2 -A3 gives 2 lines before and 3 lines after each match.

post_assessment.question: What is the key difference between grep, egrep, and fgrep?
options: grep uses basic regex, egrep uses extended regex, fgrep matches fixed strings with no regex
grep is faster, egrep is slower, fgrep is the fastest
They are identical commands with different names
grep searches files, egrep searches directories, fgrep searches networks
post_assessment.correct_answer: grep uses basic regex, egrep uses extended regex, fgrep matches fixed strings with no regex
post_assessment.explanation: grep interprets basic regular expressions (BRE), egrep (or grep -E) interprets extended regular expressions (ERE) which support +, ?, |, () without escaping, and fgrep (grep -F) treats the pattern as a fixed string with no special regex meaning.

post_assessment.question: Which command finds all lines in /var/log/auth.log that contain 'Failed password' and displays line numbers?
post_assessment.explanation: The -n flag prefixes each matching line with its line number. -l lists only filenames, -c counts matches, and --lines is not a valid grep option.

post_assessment.question: How would you search recursively for 'TODO' in all Python files under the current directory?
post_assessment.explanation: grep -r searches recursively, and --include='*.py' restricts the search to Python files only. The other options either don't search recursively, don't filter by extension, or misuse find/grep piping.

content_blocks.title: Why grep Is Your Most-Used Security Tool
content_blocks.content: Every security professional — from SOC analysts to red team operators — uses grep daily. It's not just a search command; it's the foundation of log analysis, artifact review, and data triage. When you're sifting through millions of log lines during an incident, grep is your fastest ally. Master it now, and you'll save hours on every investigation. Think of grep as your digital magnifying glass — the better you use it, the more hidden patterns you'll uncover. This lesson builds a skill you'll use every single day in cybersecurity.

content_blocks.title: Understanding grep: The Global Regular Expression Print
content_blocks.content:
grep searches input lines for matches to a given pattern and prints the matching lines. Its name comes from the ed editor command g/re/p (global regular expression print). At its core, grep takes a PATTERN and one or more FILE arguments, then outputs every line containing that pattern.

Basic usage:
  grep 'error' /var/log/syslog
  grep 'root' /etc/passwd

Common flags you should memorize:
  -i  Ignore case (case-insensitive search)
  -n  Print line numbers
  -c  Count matching lines
  -v  Invert match (show lines that DON'T match)
  -r  Recursive search through directories
  -w  Match whole words only
  -l  List only filenames with matches
  -A N  Show N lines After each match
  -B N  Show N lines Before each match
  -C N  Show N lines of Context (before and after)
  --color  Highlight the matching text

grep uses Basic Regular Expressions (BRE) by default. This means characters like ., *, ^, $ work as metacharacters, but +, ?, |, () need to be escaped with backslashes. For extended regex support without escaping, use grep -E (equivalent to egrep). For literal string matching with no regex interpretation, use grep -F (equivalent to fgrep).

In security work, you'll frequently combine grep with other commands via pipes. For example, 'cat access.log | grep "404"' or 'ps aux | grep "nginx"'. This composability is what makes grep indispensable.

content_blocks.title: Teach Me Like I'm 10: Pattern Hunting with grep
content_blocks.content:
Imagine you have a giant bookshelf with thousands of books, and you need to find every book that mentions 'dragon'. You could read every single page of every book — but that would take forever! grep is like a magical robot that reads through all the pages for you in seconds and puts a bright sticky note on every line where 'dragon' appears.

Here's how it works:
1. You tell grep WHAT to look for (the pattern, like 'dragon')
2. You tell grep WHERE to look (which files)
3. grep reads through everything and shows you every matching line

Special tricks:
- Use -i to make grep ignore whether letters are uppercase or DRAGONcase
- Use -n to show page numbers (line numbers) so you can find things again
- Use -v to do the OPPOSITE — show everything that DOESN'T have 'dragon'
- Use -c to just count how many matches there are instead of showing them
- Use --color to paint the matching word in bright red so it pops out

The coolest part? You can chain grep with other commands using pipes (|). Think of the pipe as a conveyor belt — it takes the output of one command and feeds it right into grep. Like: 'ls -la | grep secret' shows you only the files with 'secret' in their name!

content_blocks.title: Hands-On: grep Pattern Matching Exercises
content_blocks.content:
Practice grep with these real-world security scenarios. Try each command on a Linux system:

# 1. Find all failed SSH login attempts
sudo grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log

# 2. Count how many failed logins occurred
grep -c 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log

# 3. Find failed logins with case-insensitive search (some logs use different casing)
grep -i 'failed password' /var/log/auth.log

# 4. Find lines that do NOT contain 'Accepted' (filter out successful logins)
grep -v 'Accepted' /var/log/auth.log | grep 'ssh'

# 5. Show line numbers and 2 lines of context for each error in syslog
grep -n -C2 'error' /var/log/syslog

# 6. Recursively search all .conf files for 'PermitRootLogin'
grep -r --include='*.conf' 'PermitRootLogin' /etc/

# 7. Search for IP addresses using basic regex (matching patterns like 192.168.x.x)
grep -E '[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}' /var/log/auth.log

# 8. Find all unique IP addresses from SSH logs
grep 'sshd' /var/log/auth.log | grep -oE '[0-9]{1,3}(\.[0-9]{1,3}){3}' | sort -u

# 9. Show only filenames containing 'sudo' in log directory
grep -rl 'sudo' /var/log/

# 10. Use fgrep to search for a literal string with special characters
grep -F 'C:\Users\Admin' evidence.txt

content_blocks.title: Real-World: Using grep for Incident Response
content_blocks.content:
During a real incident response at a mid-size company, the SOC team noticed unusual SSH activity. They needed to quickly answer: which IPs are brute-forcing SSH, which usernames are being targeted, and has any attacker successfully logged in?

Step 1 — Identify brute force attempts:
  grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log | wc -l
  # Result: 14,832 failed attempts in 24 hours — clear brute force

Step 2 — Extract unique attacking IPs:
  grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log | grep -oE '[0-9]{1,3}(\.[0-9]{1,3}){3}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
  # Result: Top attacker IP with 12,401 attempts: 203.0.113.50

Step 3 — Find targeted usernames:
  grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log | grep -oP 'from .*? for \K\S+' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
  # Result: root (8,200), admin (3,100), ubuntu (1,500), test (1,032)

Step 4 — Check for successful compromise:
  grep 'Accepted' /var/log/auth.log | grep '203.0.113.50'
  # Result: Accepted password for ubuntu from 203.0.113.50 — COMPROMISE CONFIRMED

This four-command sequence, using only grep and basic pipes, gave the IR team everything they needed to confirm a brute force attack that escalated to a successful compromise. The entire analysis took under 60 seconds. This is why grep fluency is non-negotiable in security work.

content_blocks.title: Remembering grep Flags with the CRIME Mnemonic
content_blocks.content:
Use the mnemonic CRIME to remember the most critical grep flags:

**C** — Context: -C N (show N lines around match), -A N (after), -B N (before)
**R** — Recursive: -r (search directories recursively)
**I** — Ignore case: -i (case-insensitive matching)
**M** — Match control: -v (invert), -w (whole word), -l (filenames only), -c (count)
**E** — Extended regex: -E (egrep, use + ? | () without escaping)

Bonus flags for security work:
  -o  Only show the matching part (not the whole line) — great for extracting IPs, hashes
  -n  Line numbers — essential for referencing findings
  --include  File pattern filter — search only specific file types
  --exclude-dir  Skip directories — avoid noise from .git, node_modules

Remember: grep -Eino is your best friend for extracting IOCs from log files!

content_blocks.title: Check Your Understanding
content_blocks.content:
Take a moment to think through these questions before moving on:

1. You need to find every .py file under /opt/app that contains the word 'password'. What single grep command would you use?

2. A colleague runs 'grep ERROR application.log' and gets 500 matching lines. How would they narrow it down to only lines from today, assuming today's date appears at the start of each line in YYYY-MM-DD format?

3. Why would you use grep -F instead of plain grep when searching for a string like 'user@domain.com' in a log file?

4. You're looking for lines containing either 'ssh' OR 'telnet' in auth.log. Write two different commands that would work — one using grep -E and one using plain grep.

Write your answers down, then check: (1) grep -r --include='*.py' 'password' /opt/app, (2) grep ERROR application.log | grep '2024-01-15' (with today's date), (3) Because @ and . are regex metacharacters — -F treats them literally, (4) grep -E 'ssh|telnet' /var/log/auth.log OR grep 'ssh\|telnet' /var/log/auth.log.

content_blocks.title: From Here to Mastery
content_blocks.content: You've learned the fundamentals of grep — but the real power comes from combining it with other tools. As you progress through your cybersecurity journey, you'll find yourself building pipelines like: 'cat access.log | grep -E "(404|500)" | grep -v "favicon" | awk "{print $1}" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20'. This kind of composability is what makes the Linux command line a security professional's superpower. Practice grep daily — search through logs, filter command output, extract patterns. In the next lesson, you'll learn about environment variables and aliases, which will let you create custom shortcuts for your most-used grep commands. Keep building your muscle memory — every grep command you run makes you faster at the next incident.
